Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader is an isometric role-playing video game  developed and published by Owlcat Games set in the Warhammer 40,000 universe. The game was released for Windows, macOS, PlayStation 5, and Xbox Series X/S on December 7, 2023.

The cold light on Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. Its second DLC called Lex Imperialis was released on June 24, 2025. A third one, The Infinite Museion, was released on June 11, 2026.

Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. The game was also released on Nintendo Switch 2 on December 11, 2025. Similar to prior Owlcat games (Pathfinder: Kingmaker and Pathfinder: Wrath of the Righteous), Rogue Trader is an isometric role-playing video game, loosely based the d100 Tabletop role-playing game system from the game of the same name.

The honest version of Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) starts by giving up the comforting part. The player controls a party of up to six characters, including their own, through ground combat and social interactions. One of the game's distinguishing features is its emphasis on realm-building, with the player's decisions as a Rogue Trader affecting the rest of the gameplay as they build their space empire.

Strip Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. The alignment system allows the player to make Dogmatic choices that are typically merciless but in keeping with the setting's fervent belief in the God-Emperor, Iconoclastic choices that challenge the status quo, or Heretical choices that are Chaos-aligned. The game takes place in the Koronus Expanse, a dangerous and mostly unexplored region of space, accessible to the hegemonic Imperium of Man only through a treacherous route known as the Koronus Passage.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) shows exactly where that breaks. The chief protagonist of Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader is the titular Rogue Trader, customized from one of seven origins, a newly-found heir to the venerable Von Valancius dynasty, one of the oldest and most powerful Rogue Trader lineages still extant within the Imperium. Lady Theodora, and later the Rogue Trader themself, have in their service Abelard Werserian, the Chief Seneschal of House Von Valancius, and the unsanctioned psyker Idira Tlass.

What looks like free choice in Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) is older than choice itself. These include Jae Heydari, a smuggler and trader in illicit goods, Yrliet Lanaevyss, an Aeldari ranger, Marazhai Aezyrraesh, a Drukhari Dracon, and Ulfar, an Adeptus Astartes and member of the Space Marine Chapter the Space Wolves. The player character, a newly-discovered heir to the Von Valancius Rogue Trader dynasty, is summoned by the house's leader Lady Theodora along with other potential successors to settle the matter of inheritance.

Nobody designed the part of Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) you experience — it was inherited. The player character meets with Theodora and rival claimant Edelthrad aboard the Von Valancius flagship. Assailants led by Theodora's spymaster Kunrad Voigtvir attack the flagship and capture the player character; Voigtvir needs the player character's blood to access the Warrant of Trade, a holy relic that confers House Von Valancius's Rogue Trader status.

Every serious account of Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. When the player character proffers their blood to the flagship's computers, automated defenses are activated which drive off Voigtvir. The player character joins forces with Theodora's seneschal Abelard Werserian, unsanctioned psyker Idira Tlass, and the warrior-nun Sister Argenta.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. Edelthrad is killed in a ritual sacrifice, but the player reclaims the bridge from Voigtvir and escapes to safe space within the Koronus Expanse. With Theodora and Edelthrad dead, the rest of the dynasty quickly recognizes the player character as the new Rogue Trader.

The selfish-gene reading of Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) makes it less romantic and far more precise. The Rogue Trader finds a new Navigator for their fleet, Cassia Orsellio. Along the way, they can also enlist the services of the Magos Pasqal Haneumann and the Interrogator Heinrix Van Calox.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. The Rogue Trader also learns that their enemy is an apparent Chaos cult known as the Final Dawn. While settling matters on agricultural planet Janus, the Rogue Trader has the option of recruiting Yrliet Lanaevyss, an exiled Aeldari ranger.

The feeling that Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. After putting the house's affairs in order, the administrative headquarters of Von Valancius, planet Dargonus, is attacked by Drukhari raiders led by the Dracon Marazhai Aezyrraesh. The Rogue Trader is then led into a trap by either Yrliet, if she was recruited, or a spy of House Von Valancius, and captured by Marazhai.

Nothing in Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) was built for you — it was built for reproduction. Marazhai brings the Rogue Trader and their retinue to Comorragh, the capital city of the Drukhari, intending to use them in a ploy to gain power within the scheming aristocratic families of the city. Instead, Marazhai is stripped of his status and reduced to gladiator within the city's fighting pits, while the Rogue Trader and their cohorts are given over to a Drukhari scientist to be experimented upon.

The psychology underneath Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) is simpler and older than the story on top. The Rogue Trader is then partially dissected and abandoned in a corpse dump and left for dead. In order to escape from Comorragh, the Rogue Trader fights in the gladiatorial arena of Comorragh, potentially reuniting with each of their companions along the way, including Yrliet.

Behind Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. The player also has the option to recruit Marazhai himself, and a captive Space Marine, Ulfar of the Space Wolves. Fleeing Comorragh, the Rogue Trader returns to the Koronus Expanse to find that in their absence, a war has erupted between two rival Rogue Traders, Incendia Chorda and Calligos Winterscale.

The nihilist does not deny Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) — he only refuses to flatter it. In an effort to maintain order, the Inquisitor Xavier Calcazar has declared himself temporary warden of the Koronus Expanse and tasks the Rogue Trader with ending the conflict. After dealing with Chorda and Winterscale, Calcazar enlists the Rogue Trader to join a chapter of Space Wolves in assaulting the main stronghold of the Cult of the Final Dawn, and confronting the cult's leader, Uralon the Cruel.

What culture calls destiny in Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. Afterwards, the Rogue Trader returns to Calcazar's office to find him gone, and learns from an agent of his that the Inquisitor has left the Koronus Expanse. If any of Chorda, Winterscale, or Uralon are still alive and the Rogue Trader is of the correct ideological alignment, they can also be recruited.

The genes do not care about Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game); they care about copies. Chasing after Calcazar, the Rogue Trader goes through a dimensional gate and arrives in a remote system filled with Necrons. The Rogue Trader lands on a Tomb World and confronts Calcazar, who is in the process of subduing a C'tan, a type of pure energy being with godlike abilities that were defeated by the Necrons millennia ago and shattered into various shards.

Take away the meaning and Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) still functions — that is the disturbing part. Calcazar explains that long ago, he, Theodora, and a member of the Adeptus Mechanicus, Archmagos Amarnat (of which Pasqal is a clone with a fragment of Amarnat's mind), discovered a shard of the Void Dragon C'tan on the then-asleep Tomb World. The three worked together to form a plan to activate the shard and reform the C'tan, with the shared goal of leashing the awakened C'tan and using its immense power for themselves.

The unconscious does not argue with Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game); it simply acts first. This plan required technology beyond even Amarnat's capabilities, so Calcazar worked with the Drukhari, which led to the Dark Eldar raids on the Koronus Expanse and brought Dargonus to the attention of Marazhai. Meanwhile Lady Theodora started experimenting with and fell to Chaos, resulting in her death when Argenta discovered her with a Chaos relic and killed her.

Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. While researching the Necron technologies of the Tomb World, Theodora also inadvertently destroyed the Aeldari Craftworld Crudarach, Yrliet's homeworld, thus resulting in her exile. Now with technology recovered from the Cult of the Final Dawn's stronghold thanks to the Rogue Trader and the Space Wolves, Calcazar has finally completed the device and is ready to summon and bind the shard of the Void Dragon, ostensibly in service to the Inquisition.

The bleak reading of Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) is also the most testable one. The player can choose to either ally with Calcazar or fight him. Afterwards, the Rogue Trader will have the choice of destroying the C'tan, swearing loyalty to it and joining it in submission as it prepares to devour the Koronus Expanse, or either allowing Calcazar to use the device to imprison the C'tan or doing it themself.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game). An epilogue then details the various fates of the Rogue Trader, their companions, the numerous other inhabitants and planets of the Koronus Expanse, and the ramifications of the player's many choices throughout the game. A hidden concurrent subplot throughout the game details the formation of a new C'tan that becomes known as Nomos.

The self that experiences Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) is a committee, not a king. If the player manages to make specific choices throughout the game and find Theodora's hidden data caches regarding the Necron technology, this being, named Nomos, quickly learns and begins to view the Rogue Trader as a parental figure, internalizing the player's choice of moral alignment. Later, Nomos will transfer its mind from the frigate's computers to a physical body, allowing it to accompany the Rogue Trader during the final confrontation with Calcazar.

Reproduction explains more of Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) than any philosophy dares to admit. After defeating the awakened C'tan, the Rogue Trader can then allow Nomos to consume the C'tan shard and absorb its power to become a newborn C'tan, which will act depending on the Rogue Trader's ideological conviction to further the power of House Von Valancius. Rogue Trader received generally positive reviews upon release, according to review aggregator Metacritic.

Once you see Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader (video game) as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. In Japan, four critics from Famitsu gave the game a total score of 28 out of 40. Rock, Paper, Shotgun applauded the alignment system, citing that both extremes and the middle of the road options had playable value.
